title: Japan Doesn't Use Enough Robots*
subtitle: *Interpreting real world evidence from Japan regarding transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) treatment.
text:
My daughter loves Japan. I'm not quite sure why, but she does. She ask questions along these lines:

“Mommy, when I was in your tummy, did you know I would love Japan?”

She's learning Japanese on Duolingo and has made us promise to take her to Japan when she's 10. She loves sushi and wants sushi every Sunday. We have family dinner on Sunday, but if we had family dinner every night, she would probably also request Sushi then too.

All of that is beside the point. Today, I'm attempting to get more readers in Japan—or maybe just please my daughter. That's not the real reason. It's even more trivial than that! I wondered what would happen if I just tried to write a review article about the first thing that Google Scholar suggested I read. And so when I opened Google Scholar to embark on this quixotic mission, the first article presented was the one I'm gonna review with my readers today. It's about real-world outcomes on transcranial. Magnetic stimulation in Japan, so I came up with the funny title at the top.

To be clear, Japan loves its robots. I love Japanese robots. In Japan, everybody's on board with robots, at least in theory. Then I read the following paper:

Real-world outcome of rTMS treatment for depression within the Japanese public health insurance system: registry data from Kansai TMS network

What a great title! I also recently co-authored a paper on accelerated TMS, in pre-print out of the Acacia Clinics site, and I'm including a link to it here. I bring that other paper up not because I'm a deranged narcissist but because the sample size is relevant.

This large-scale data from Japan? It reports on…

102 patients with depression who received rTMS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex

The paper we just got out the door from Acacia clinics reports on accelerated TMS included:

226 individuals treated in an outpatient clinic

If one northern California clinic—doing a more labor-intensive version of transcranial magnetic stimulation, which isn’t always done with a robot arm but sometimes it is—can lap 5 hospitals in Japan, we have a problem. Is this the one time Japan needs to fall more deeply in love with robots?

It’s a robot and a brain stimulator.

I am going to start with the assertion that Japan Loves Robots. My readers know I like to back up a claim! There is data on the attitudes towards robots in Japan from papers with titles like— and this is true1:

Does Japan really have robot mania? Comparing attitudes by implicit and explicit measures

Yes, there is data on how into robots the Japanese are. The first data I will present is also my favorite. The study use both self-report measures and implicit association tasks. Implicit association tasks measure what we really think in the milliseconds before conscious thought can get in the way of communicating our unconscious biases. My favorite fact from this table is that individuals below age 43.9 have an explicit preference for robots, according to self-report, and an implicit fear of robots, according to the implicit association task. Across self-reports, Japanese-only male respondents also find robots both preferable and more threatening. There is, additionally, an implicit association with robots being threatening. In Japan, robots are both loved and feared. I can't get enough of this. I think I'm a lot like members of the male Japanese public—I welcome our robot overlords, but I think it's pretty clear that the humans are dead over any reasonable time frame.

Before my readers start arguing with me about the fact that a preference for robots might not translate into the healthcare domain, there is also data from Japan on that:

Acceptability of robots for home health care.

Compared to respondents in Ireland and Finland, Japanese respondents are overwhelmingly more open to using homecare robots, both for their families and for themselves. This should be the key market for Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation. In a culture that pioneered ritual suicide and samurai carried a spare sword expressly to preserve the option to kill themselves, you imagine a robot-ish solution to a depression problem would be a big deal.2

By the way, I'm not kidding about that long history of ritual suicide thing—this is what Google AI generated for me…

A samurai committing seppuku would plunge either a wakizashi, tachi, or tanto into their gut and slice horizontally. Then, they would remove the blade and stab themselves in the heart or slash across their own throat to ensure death.

In a delicious moment of irony, that particular AI summary of the answer to the question is self-aggrandizing and historically inaccurate. The point of the wakizashi was to allow for a samurai to start a ritual suicide— and then one of their underlings could put them out of their misery quickly—because they were writhing in pain and going to die anyway, and thus their underlings got a pass on killing their lord. It was an entitled way for samurai to get someone else to dispatch them without having the dishonor on their head. Thanks, Google AI, for creating self-aggrandizing robot propaganda—but some humans are still here to call you out on your BS. I’m like the “Sarah Connor” of health-satire newsletters.

Now, getting on to the data from our Japanese TMS study, it followed consecutive patients in five hospitals in Japan and looked at the outcomes of Transcranial. Magnetic Stimulation Treatment for depression. In brief, it was really good:

43.1% of patients got into remission, and another 13.7% had a response of 50%3—this response date? In a pharmaceutical trial would be considered a success on its own

Transcranial magnetic stimulation replicates, over and over again, in every country I've looked at treatment-resistant depression. It’s cost-effective, too—even in Japan specifically.4

Transcranial magnetic stimulation is a safe and effective—and cost-effective—intervention for depression on a public health scale. my colleagues at Acacia Clinics and Fermata in New York have demonstrated, over and over again5, that this can be done rapidly as well. Now, SAINT neuromodulation has an FDA-breakthrough clearance and is commercially available.

The only thing lacking is appropriate payment models to get this remarkable public health intervention, with no medication necessary and limited adverse effects to the appropriate scale to address the mental health crisis meaningfully.

On a scale of over 1700 patients, my colleagues and I have relentlessly published on the potent nature of this modality for depression6. We have also done the same diligent work to document its remarkable and durable efficacy in OCD—even leading to remission in many real-world patients.

This treatment is not experimental or unproven. It's relentlessly proven globally. It's time to start demanding appropriate payment for this modality from every payer without the prior authorization barriers currently in place. It’s even a finalist for the Health Value Awards.

It's underutilized in Japan and is the one kind of robot-ish thing that is underutilized. That part was just a hook. I don't really have much more to say about it other than thinking it's hilarious.
